lines.text: Welcome to Voice Lab, the show where we hand a script a stack of text and get a finished conversation back. I am Reginald.
And I am Deja. Today we are looking at the tool that made this very episode: two Python scripts, a manuscript, and nothing else.
Voice Lab clones a voice from one consented recording and speaks any text with it, and it all runs locally on your machine.
There are two entry points. Generate voice dot py is the one-shot helper: one voice file, one sentence, one audio file.
Make sentences dot py is the interactive one. You pick a voice, type lines at a prompt, and switch speakers by entering a number.
But today we are using the third option, generate manuscript dot py, which renders a whole JSON manuscript in one run.
A manuscript declares named voices, each pointing at a consented WAV or MP3 reference, and then an ordered list of lines that cite those voices.
The format itself is written up as a skill file, in the agents skills folder, so an agent can read it and write a valid manuscript for you.
That means you can describe the scene in plain English, and the skill defines the rules: which fields exist, how settings nest, and how errors are reported.
Every episode you hear is one of these manuscripts. Two voices, eleven lines, and a single command that also joins everything into one file.
So install it by initializing the submodule, running the Raven setup script, and accepting the model terms. Then render your first manuscript.
That is Voice Lab for this episode. Write your script, pick your voices, and press play. Goodbye.
